newsitem.title: USA: D.C. board slams city procurement, pension debt.
newsitem.headline: D.C. board slams city procurement, pension debt.

text.p: The District of Columbia's financial control board has called for major changes in the way the city procures outside services and in how Congress deals with the city's multi-billion unfunded pension liability.
The five-member control board had pledged to issue the recommendations after it released a "strategic plan" in December 1996.

The board describes "significant problems" in the District's procurement operations and in the huge pension liability that the city inherited from the federal government when it won home rule in the mid-1970s.
The reports call for "constructive and, often far-reaching changes" in both areas, the board said in a statement.
The report describes D.C.'s procurement operations as "essentially broken."
After reviewing 4,200 contracts submitted to the city for approval, the panel concluded that the city overpays for services.

The city often exceeds its spending authority for services, "splits" procurements to avoid reviews that are required by law, "plans poorly when it plans at all," and inadequately trains employees undertaking the contracting, it said.

Meanwhile, the city's 13-member council urged President Clinton not to drop the $660 million payment that D.C. gets in lieu of taxes each year from the federal government when he releases a proposed federal aid program for the city next week.

In a letter to Franklin Raines, director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the council said it was worried that it could lose the federal payment even if Congress does not clear all of the OMB's proposed aid for the city.
